title: Ram Charan's Peddi Just Landed on Netflix. Here's Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: After a ₹340 crore theatrical run that dominated Andhra Pradesh but stumbled everywhere else, the three-hour Telugu sports epic gets its second chance — and for NRIs who missed it in cinemas, this is the version that matters.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Peddi grossed ₹340 crore worldwide, with strong performance in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
  • The film is now streaming on Netflix, making it accessible for the Indian diaspora.
  • Ram Charan's performance as a para-athlete highlights themes of recognition and identity.
  • Despite mixed box office reviews, Telugu audiences consider Peddi a hit.
  • The film's three-hour runtime suits the streaming format, allowing for flexible viewing.

The opening shot of Peddi is a sugarcane field at dawn, green and endless, the kind of rural India that rarely makes it to a Netflix thumbnail. By the time the credits roll three hours later, that field has given way to a prosthetic blade, a national running track, and a man screaming at the Indian government to acknowledge his village exists.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=sF2dj7ycZvA

This is not a subtle film. It's also not easy to forget.

Ram Charan plays a gifted sugarcane laborer in Andhra Pradesh who rises first as a wrestler, then — after a bitter rival destroys his leg — as a blade-running para-track athlete. Directed by Buchi Babu Sana (whose debut *Uppena* announced him as one of Telugu cinema's most physical filmmakers), Peddi is an unabashedly maximalist sports drama: operatic in its emotions, brutal in its action, and anchored by a lead performance that reminds you why Ram Charan is one of the most watchable actors in Indian cinema when he commits to a role.

> "In North America, it hit $3.4 million in just 13 days, making it the highest-grossing Telugu film of 2026 in that market."

> "If people can't see my village on a map, I'll make them hear its name on a track." — Ram Charan as Peddi

Janhvi Kapoor plays the wealthy politician's daughter who falls for him — a romance that is both entirely predictable and, in the film's best moments, disarmingly tender. Shiva Rajkumar lends veteran gravity as a mentor figure. The supporting cast across the Telugu and dubbed versions is stacked.

The Box Office Story

![Andhra Pradesh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Tirumala_090615.jpg/3840px-Tirumala_090615.jpg)

Peddi's theatrical run was a study in contradictions. In Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, the film was enormous — ₹219 crore in gross collections, more than 118,000 tracked shows, and an opening day of ₹82.50 crore that made it Ram Charan's second-biggest opener after RRR. In North America, it hit $3.4 million in just 13 days, making it the highest-grossing Telugu film of 2026 in that market.

But the pan-India dream never materialized. The Hindi dub collapsed early. Tamil and Malayalam dubbed versions barely registered. Against a production budget of ₹350 crore, the worldwide gross settled at approximately ₹340 crore — a loss in industry math, even as nearly 3.92 million tickets were sold on BookMyShow alone.

The trade called it an underperformer. Telugu audiences called it a hit. Both were right.

Why Netflix Changes Everything

Streaming Impact for NRIs
›Available in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam.
›No showtimes or sold-out screens.
›Flexible viewing: pause, rewind, and break up the film.
›Addresses themes of identity and recognition for the diaspora.

For the Indian diaspora, Peddi's arrival on Netflix today — available in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam — is arguably the more significant event. The theatrical window for Indian films in North American multiplexes is punishingly short. A week, maybe two, and the screens flip to the next release. If you didn't catch Peddi during its opening weekend in June, you likely didn't catch it at all.

Netflix erases that problem. No showtimes. No sold-out IMAX screens. No three-hour commitment you can't pause. For NRIs across the US, UK, Canada, and the Gulf, this is the version of Peddi that will define how they experience the film — on their couch, on their timeline, with subtitles if they need them.

And the film genuinely rewards the streaming format. Its three-hour runtime, which felt indulgent in a theatre seat, works differently at home. You can break it up. You can rewind the action sequences (and you will want to — the wrestling choreography is extraordinary). You can pause during the film's heavier emotional beats and come back when you're ready.

The Diaspora Angle

Peddi is, at its core, a story about a man demanding that the system see his people. That his village — invisible, unrecognized, literally absent from government records — deserves a railway station, deserves to exist on a map. He uses sport as a megaphone, his body as proof of what his community can produce.

For NRIs who left small-town India and built lives abroad, that particular ache — the feeling that the place you came from is invisible to the larger world — tends to land differently. Peddi may be set in the sugarcane belts of Andhra, but its emotional frequency travels.

Peddi is now streaming on Netflix across all markets. Available in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam with subtitles.
